<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-summary">Summary</button></h2><div id="work-acc-summary" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Gāthāsaptaśatī is a collection of 700 verses in the gāthā (song) form, written by the Sanskrit poet Sātavāhana. The work covers a range of topics, including love, nature, social satire, and morality. Gāthāsaptaśatī is known for its simple and direct language, vivid imagery, and use of metaphor. The poems are often brief and present a range of emotions and experiences, from the joys of love to the pains of separation. Many of the verses contain moral lessons and advice on how to live a good life, and some of the poems also contain Buddhist themes and ideas. The collection is divided into seven sections, each containing 100 verses, and each section is named after a different bird, including the Cakravāka (the Indian cuckoo), Śārikā (the Indian lark), and the Vāsantatilaka (the Indian peafowl). The names of the birds are used as a metaphor to convey different moods and emotions, with the cuckoo symbolizing love and the peafowl representing beauty and grace. Gāthāsaptaśatī is an important work in Sanskrit literature, known for its literary and cultural value, and has been widely translated into various languages. It is a testament to the enduring legacy of Sātavāhana's work that it continues to be read and appreciated by people around the world today.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-contents">Contents</button></h2><div id="work-acc-contents" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Gāthāsaptaśatī, a collection of 700 verses in the gāthā (song) form, covers a wide range of topics in Sanskrit literature. The poems in the collection are characterized by their simplicity and directness, and often contain vivid imagery and metaphor. Some of the common themes found in the Gāthāsaptaśatī include: Love and Romance: Many of the verses in the collection deal with the joys and pains of love. Sātavāhana uses imagery such as flowers, birds, and the moon to describe the beauty of his beloved, and laments the pain of separation and longing.<br><br>Nature: Sātavāhana was clearly inspired by the natural world around him, and many of the verses in the Gāthāsaptaśatī describe the beauty of the natural world, including mountains, rivers, trees, and animals.<br><br>Morality: The collection also contains poems that offer moral lessons and advice on how to live a good life. These verses often use simple stories and anecdotes to illustrate important moral values, such as honesty, kindness, and selflessness.<br><br>Social Satire: Some of the verses in the collection are satirical in nature, poking fun at human foibles and weaknesses. Sātavāhana uses humor and irony to comment on the social and political realities of his time.<br><br>Buddhist Themes: While it is not clear whether Sātavāhana was a Buddhist monk or follower of the Buddhist tradition, some of the poems in the collection contain Buddhist themes and ideas, including the impermanence of all things, the importance of mindfulness, and the concept of Karma.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-uniqueness">Uniqueness</button></h2><div id="work-acc-uniqueness" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Gāthāsaptaśatī is a unique work in Sanskrit literature for several reasons. Firstly, the collection contains 700 verses, which is a large number for a single work in the gāthā (song) form. Secondly, the poems are notable for their simplicity and directness, using vivid imagery and metaphor to convey a range of emotions and experiences. Thirdly, the collection covers a wide range of themes, including love, nature, morality, social satire, and even some Buddhist themes and ideas. Finally, the use of bird names as section titles adds a layer of poetic beauty and metaphorical meaning to the work. Overall, the Gāthāsaptaśatī is a testament to the enduring legacy of Sanskrit poetry, and continues to be appreciated by readers around the world for its literary and cultural value.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-contribution">Contribution &amp; Notes</button></h2><div id="work-acc-contribution" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Gāthāsaptaśatī is a significant contribution to Sanskrit literature for several reasons. Firstly, the collection showcases the versatility and richness of the gāthā form, which had previously been used primarily for religious or epic poetry. Secondly, the work is a valuable source of insights into the literary, cultural, and philosophical traditions of ancient India, offering glimpses into the social and political realities of the time. Thirdly, the work has influenced subsequent generations of poets, both in India and abroad, and continues to be appreciated for its poetic beauty and universal themes.<br><br>Apart from its literary and cultural significance, the Gāthāsaptaśatī is also notable for its historical context. While the exact date of its composition is not known, scholars believe that it was written during the 1st century CE, around the same time as other important works in Sanskrit literature. The collection is also believed to have originated in the Deccan region of South India, which was a center of cultural and intellectual activity during this period. Additionally, the work has been the subject of extensive scholarship and analysis, with scholars examining its language, themes, and historical context. Today, the Gāthāsaptaśatī continues to be appreciated by readers for its poetic beauty, universal themes, and valuable insights into the cultural and philosophical traditions of ancient India.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-quotations">Quotable Quotations</button></h2><div id="work-acc-quotations" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">ते विरलाः सत्पुरुषाः स्नेहो येषामभिन्नमुखरागः । अनुदिवसवर्धमानः पुत्रेष्वृणमिव हि सङ्क्रामेत् ॥ \[गाथासप्तशती - २.१३\] te viralāḥ satpuruṣāḥ sneho yeṣāmabhinnamukharāgaḥ । anudivasavardhamānaḥ putreṣvṛṇamiva hi saṅkrāmet ॥ \[gāthāsaptaśatī - 2.13\]<br>They are rarely good men, in whose friendships the attachment does not fade but increases every day.  Such affection should be continued  to the next generation just like a father's debt.</div></div></div>
